analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to cover employees' families or pay a tax funding health insurance for pregnant women and children.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in three House committees and four subcommittees until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every employer to enroll employees and their families in a certified health plan or pay a 3.2% payroll tax (plus a 1% tax on the employee) that would fund state-run health plans covering pregnant women and children who have no other coverage. States would have had to offer preventive care, hospital and doctor services, mental health care, and prescription drugs with limits on deductibles and co-pays, and premium subsidies for low-income families. It also would have barred insurers selling small-employer plans from refusing customers or setting prices based on health status, backed by a 50% excise tax on plans that broke the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured pregnant women, children, and newborns, who would be automatically enrolled in a state plan with a guaranteed benefit package; low-income families, who could get help with premiums, deductibles, and co-pays; and workers at small businesses, who would gain access to plans that could not turn them away or price them by health status.

how_it_helps.text: Every state would have to establish a plan covering pregnant women and children not enrolled in a qualified employer or federal plan, with preventive care including immunizations and prenatal care, major medical services, and extended services like mental health care, with no limits on amount, duration, or scope [S3].
Low-income enrollees could apply for assistance to limit or eliminate premiums, deductibles, and co-pays, and newborns and children relinquished to agencies would be automatically enrolled [S3].
Qualified health plans could not deny coverage for required services based on health status, medical history, or lack of insurability, and could not exclude pre-existing conditions [S3].

Small-employer plans would have to be guaranteed renewable for 12-month terms and could not discriminate based on health status or claims experience, with premiums community-rated within geographic areas, enforced by a 50% excise tax on gross premiums [S2].

Employers who did not provide coverage would pay a 3.2% payroll tax on each uncovered employee and a $100-per-day penalty for failing to submit enrollment information to the state, with the revenue funding the new state plans through a dedicated trust fund [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, through the 3.2% payroll tax or the cost of certified family coverage; employees without employer coverage, through a 1% wage tax; health insurers, through certification standards, guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules on the small-employer market, and a 50% excise tax on noncompliant plans; and medical providers, because the state plans would reimburse at Medicare-style payment rates.

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax and coverage mandate would raise labor costs for every employer, phasing in from large employers in 1995 to small employers in 1998, and small employers would only be able to meet the requirement through insured plans, not self-insured ones [S3].
State plans would pay providers at Medicare-based rates with no administrative or judicial review of those rates, which could push doctors and hospitals to limit participation and strain access [S3].
The bill would preempt state laws that require richer benefits or different coverage rules for pregnant women and children in employer plans, overriding states that currently mandate more [S3].

After full phase-in, individuals who failed to enroll and showed no good cause could owe their state twice the premiums they would have paid on time, and enrollment could not be freely terminated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a large, concrete benefit: near-universal coverage for pregnant women and children with strong consumer protections, paid for by a broad employer tax rather than a deficit. The honest costs are real: new taxes on employers of every size, lower Medicare-style payment rates that could tighten provider supply, and federal preemption of state benefit mandates. It was also a very complex design, enrolling whole families through employers and states with elaborate coordination rules, and it relied on the 1993 political moment passing any employer mandate at all, which it did not.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, then bounced to four subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Matsui (D-CA) introduced the Children and Pregnant Women Health Insurance Act of 1993 on February 2, 1993 [S1].
It was referred jointly to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor on February 2, 1993 [S5].

Between February 8 and February 24, 1993, it was referred to four subcommittees: Health, Labor-Management Relations, Commerce Consumer Protection and Competitiveness, and Health and the Environment [S5].
No further action is recorded; the bill sat at the subcommittee level for the remainder of the 103rd Congress, which ended January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers, who never faced the payroll tax, the coverage mandate, or the small-market rating rules, and who kept the pre-ACA system in which coverage for pregnant women and children depended on employer benefits or state programs. Uninsured families gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers avoided the mandate

sides.party_line_note: Every recorded supporter was a Democrat — the sponsor and 27 Democratic cosponsors — and the bill never reached a vote where party splits could be counted [S4].

industries.note: Employers would owe a 3.2% payroll tax per uncovered employee (with a matching 1% employee tax) or the cost of certified family coverage, plus $100-per-day penalties for failing to submit state enrollment forms. The industry's cost in this bill is precisely the funding for public coverage, so its interest runs against the bill's beneficiaries.

The bill would make insurers and qualified plans the permanent channel for both employer-based and state-plan coverage, including administration of the state plans through insurance companies, while locking in rules: certification standards, guaranteed issue, community rating, and a 50% excise tax on noncompliant small-employer plans. Insurers gain a large guaranteed market but give up underwriting and risk-based pricing.

Small employers would be phased in last (1998) and could only satisfy the mandate through insured plans, not self-insurance, leaving them dependent on carriers facing new rating and benefit rules. Their added cost funds the coverage expansion, so their interest runs against the public's gain in this bill.

State plans would reimburse providers at Medicare-based rates with no review of those rates, cutting payments below typical private rates, while guaranteeing millions of previously uninsured pregnant women and children as paying patients.
